nameStory: This cricket carries the name of August Johann Rösel von Rosenhof, an 18th-century German entomologist who was famous for his detailed illustrations of insects. The 'bush-cricket' part of its name reflects its preference for living among shrubs and tall grasses rather than on the ground like many of its cricket cousins.
description: Roesel's Bush-cricket is a robust, medium-sized member of the katydid family that's become established in New England after arriving from Europe. These stocky crickets are typically brown or green with a distinctive yellow edge along their wing covers, and they're about the size of your thumb. Unlike the long, thin antennae of typical katydids, these bush-crickets have a more compact build with relatively short wings that often don't cover their entire abdomen. You'll hear their distinctive buzzing song on warm summer evenings as males call from their perches in dense vegetation.

idTips.label: Yellow wing edges
idTips.description: Look for bright yellow or cream-colored borders along the wing covers (forewings) that create a distinctive stripe down each side - this yellow edge feels slightly raised and waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Compact body shape
idTips.description: The body feels solid and chunky compared to other katydids, with a broad thorax that gives it an almost armored appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Short wings
idTips.description: Wings often don't reach the tip of the abdomen, giving it a stubby appearance - the wing texture is leathery rather than papery thin

idTips.label: Buzzing song
idTips.description: Males produce a continuous mechanical buzzing sound that lasts 10-20 seconds, like a tiny motorcycle revving - much different from the chirping of ground crickets

idTips.label: Brown-green coloring
idTips.description: Body ranges from olive green to rich brown, often with a mottled pattern that feels slightly rough and bumpy rather than smooth

habitat: You'll find Roesel's Bush-crickets in areas with dense, tall grasses and shrubby vegetation, especially in meadows, field edges, and overgrown areas with plenty of cover. They particularly favor spots where grasses mix with low bushes and brambles, often in slightly disturbed habitats like abandoned lots or the margins of agricultural areas. Look for them in sunny to partially shaded locations where the vegetation creates a thick tangle about knee to waist high.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet present - eggs laid the previous fall are developing in the soil and plant debris.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity begins in mid-July when adults emerge and begin their buzzing courtship songs, which are most noticeable during warm evenings.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, continuing to sing and mate until the first hard frosts, when females lay eggs for next year's generation.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - the species overwinters as eggs hidden in soil and dead vegetation.

funFact: Despite being European natives, Roesel's Bush-crickets are actually expanding their range northward due to climate change, and they're such recent arrivals to New England that many field guides from the 1990s don't even mention them - you might be spotting a species that's still actively colonizing our region!
confusionNotes: The yellow wing edges are your best bet for distinguishing Roesel's from other bush-crickets and katydids in New England - no other local species has that distinctive bright yellow stripe running along the wing covers. Remember: 'Yellow edges equal Roesel's!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cricket,' this species is actually more closely related to katydids than to the crickets you might hear chirping at night - it's a naming confusion that reflects how Europeans originally classified these insects before scientists understood their relationships better.
compareHints: Since Roesel's is the only species in its genus in New England, compare it to other bush-crickets in the katydid family by looking for those signature yellow wing edges - other local katydids either lack this feature entirely or have much more subtle coloration along their wing borders. The robust, compact build also sets it apart from the more delicate, long-winged true katydids you might encounter.
